approved: Customs Amendment (Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2014
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
This bill changes customs rules so goods from Korea can receive lower duties under a trade deal.
It sets tests for when products count as originating in Korea and puts duties on exporters and producers who seek the preferential rate.
The new rules start on the later of 1 December 2014 or the day the agreement begins for Australia.
The bill creates rules of origin for Korean goods imported into Australia.
It requires exporters of Australian goods to Korea and producers of those goods to meet obligations for preferential duty claims.
It amends the Customs Act 1901 to enable preferential rates of customs duty for qualifying goods.
Exporters and producers of Australian goods sent to Korea, and importers of Korean goods into Australia, are affected.

Introduced the Customs Amendment (Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2014, which implements Australia's rules of origin obligations under the agreement, noting goods liberalisation alone is estimated to add nearly $5 billion to Australia's GDP between 2015 and 2030.

Introduced the complementary Customs Tariff Amendment (Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2014, which sets duty-free access and preferential tariff rates for Korean-originating goods, phasing these rates to zero by 2021.

Supported the Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement bills as on balance in the national interest, citing forecasts of $3½ billion more in exports and 1,745 additional jobs by 2015, but moved an amendment urging the government to renegotiate the deal to remove investor-state dispute settlement provisions, protect labour market regulation and reverse automotive industry funding cuts.
Referred the Customs Amendment and Customs Tariff Amendment bills implementing the Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement to the Federation Chamber for further consideration.

Reported that the Human Rights Committee examined 12 bills, found nine required no further scrutiny, deferred one and identified two for further examination; it concluded that 10 of 12 matters concerning the Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment (2014 Budget Measures No. 2) Bill 2014 were compatible with human rights.

Supported the Customs Amendment (Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement Implementation) Bill 2014, detailing tariff eliminations across beef, dairy, wine and horticulture, and forecasting KAFTA would add $5 billion in additional income between 2015 and 2030 while creating 1,700 jobs in its first year of operation.

Argued that the best defence for Australian agriculture against the power of supermarkets is to develop strong export markets, welcoming the Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement as an imperfect but important step toward a more profitable Australian agricultural economy.

Supported the Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement, noting two-way trade with Korea was worth $32.1 billion in 2013, that 84 per cent of Australian exports would become tariff-free immediately rising to 99.8 per cent, and citing endorsements from the Export Council of Australia and Australian Pork Limited.

Supported the Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement's tariff benefits for the farmers, miners and fishers of O'Connor, citing an estimated $5 billion in additional GDP between 2015 and 2030 and elimination of Korea's 40 per cent tariff on beef over 15 years, but also warned the deal adds further pressure on an already struggling Australian automotive industry.

Discussed the Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement bill, noting the deal is expected to create about 1,700 jobs in its first year and boost the economy by $650 million after 15 years, while raising Labor's concerns about investor-state dispute settlement clauses that let corporations sue governments over policies harming their investments.

Opposed the Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement because it included investor-state dispute settlement, limited parliamentary scrutiny and lacked adequate analysis of intellectual property and manufacturing effects. Supported trade in products such as beef, wine and agricultural goods, but argued that foreign corporations should not be able to challenge Australian laws through private arbitration.

Announced that the bill would amend the Customs Tariff Act 1995 to implement Australia's tariff commitments under the Korea-Australia Free Trade Agreement. Supported the agreement as opening markets, strengthening competitiveness and creating opportunities for exporters, workers, consumers and investors, and said it should deliver benefits once parliamentary procedures were completed.
